description:
What Are AI Agents?
You've probably heard about AI agents and how they're changing the game for knowledge work.
This course breaks down what agents actually are and how they're different from regular AI
workflows .
AI agents are applications built on generative AI that can reason over and generate natural
language, automate tasks by using tools, and respond to contextual conditions to take
appropriate action .
The Core Distinction
System What It Does Autonomy
Chatbot/Assistant Responds to queries None - waits for input
Automation Script Follows fixed rules None - predetermined
AI Agent Pursues goals, uses tools, adapts Some - plans and acts
What You Will Learn
By the end of this 5-day course, you will be able to:
Understand what AI agents are and how they differ from regular AI workflows
Identify the building blocks that make agents autonomous
Distinguish between AI assistants, AI agents, and agentic AI
Understand agent architecture and design patterns
Determine when to use AI agents (and when not to)
Implement agents in your workplace
Prerequisites
None. This course is designed for beginners with no coding background required .

lessons.title: The Three Levels of AI Systems
lessons.content:
To understand AI agents, we need to understand three basic levels of AI systems :
Level 1: Large Language Models (LLMs)
A large language model is essentially a "super language engine" — given input, it outputs text. It's
passive, has no memory, and doesn't take action .
Examples: GPT, Claude, DeepSeek, Qwen
Level 2: AI Assistants
An AI assistant wraps a large model with an interactive interface and memory management. It can
handle multi-turn conversations, but it's still fundamentally "human asks, AI answers" — the
boundary of execution stops at text response .
Examples: ChatGPT, Siri, Alexa, Copilot
Level 3: AI Agents
An AI agent is an AI system that can autonomously perceive its environment, independently
make plans, call tools, execute actions, and dynamically adjust strategies based on feedback .
Simple Analogy:
LLM = The "brain"
AI Assistant = The "talking brain"
AI Agent = A "digital employee who can act, collaborate, and learn"

lessons.title: Core Characteristics of AI Agents
lessons.content:
AI agents have four core characteristics :
Characteristic Description
Autonomous Goal
Decomposition

task sequences

and even other AI models
Closed-Loop Action Forms a complete autonomous decision cycle: "perceive →
plan → act → feedback → revise"
Persistent Memory & State
Management
Can maintain context across sessions, like a real "working"
role

lessons.title: The Three Components of an AI Agent
lessons.content:
AI agents have three key elements :
Component 1: Large Language Model (The Brain)
The LLM is the agent's brain — it uses generative AI for language understanding and reasoning .
Component 2: Instructions (The Job Description)
Instructions are a system prompt that defines the agent's role and behavior. Think of it as the
agent's job description .
Component 3: Tools (The Hands)
Tools are what the agent uses to interact with the world :
Tool Type Purpose Examples
Knowledge Tools Access information Search engines, databases
Action Tools Perform tasks Sending emails, updating calendars

lessons.title: The Agent Reasoning Loop
lessons.content:
Agents operate in a loop of reasoning and acting :
Reason → Act → Observe → Repeat
1. Reason: Agent decides what to do next
2. Act: Agent takes an action (like calling a tool)
3. Observe: Agent observes the result
4. Repeat: Agent decides whether to take another action or provide a final response
This loop continues until the agent's goal is accomplished or it reaches a stopping condition .

lessons.title: Retrieval and Tool Integration
lessons.content:
Retrieval Systems
Retrieval allows agents to access external knowledge sources, such as documents and databases,
to generate more accurate and informative responses .
Tool Integration
Tool integration enables agents to perform actions in the world :
Calling APIs
Querying databases
Executing code
Interacting with other systems
Frameworks That Enable Agents
Framework Purpose
ReAct Couples reasoning and acting in a unified loop
RAG Retrieval-Augmented Generation — grounds responses in factual data

lessons.title: Programming Patterns for Agentic Systems

Pattern Description
Prompt Chaining Linking prompts where each step's output feeds the next
Routing Decision-making by LLMs
Parallelization Concurrent prompt execution
Evaluation Self-assessment of outputs

lessons.content:

AI

lessons.title: Workflows vs. Agents
lessons.content:
Aspect Workflow Agent
Path Predefined sequence Decides its own path
Flexibility Rigid Adaptive
Autonomy None Some to full
Use Case Predictable tasks Open-ended goals
Key Insight: Agentic workflows follow a specific sequence of steps managed by an augmented
LLM, while autonomous agents are given a task and decide independently on their course of
action .

lessons.title: The Assistant vs. Agent Distinction in Practice
lessons.content:
A system is behaving like an assistant when it :
Produces suggestions or explanations
Does not take repository actions
Requires the user to apply each step manually
A system is behaving like an agent when it can :
Maintain a goal across multiple steps
Decide intermediate actions
Create or modify durable artifacts
Iterate based on feedback signals

lessons.title: Multi-Agent Systems
lessons.content:
Agents can work with one another in multi-agent systems :
One agent might gather data
Another might analyze it
A third might take action
Together, they form an AI-powered workforce that can handle complex workflows, just like a
human team .
Agents communicate with each other through prompts, using generative AI to determine what
tasks are required and which agents are responsible for completing them .

lessons.title: Agent Architecture Overview
lessons.content:
A practical course on AI agents covers these architectural topics :
Topic Description
Agent Design Template A reusable structure for designing agents
Topic Description

Hard-coded vs. LLM-determined Design When to fix behavior vs. let the LLM decide
Multi-Agent Architectures Designing systems with multiple agents

lessons.title: Design Patterns for AI Agents
lessons.content:
Pattern 1: Prompt Chaining
Prompt chaining sequences reasoning within a single agent — each step's output feeds the next,
keeping the LLM focused on one analytical problem at a time .
When to use: Your workflow has natural stages where each step depends on the previous step's
output .
Pattern 2: Routing
Routing involves decision-making by LLMs — directing requests to the appropriate handler based
on the request type .
Pattern 3: Parallelization
Parallelization executes prompts concurrently to improve throughput .
Pattern 4: Evaluation
Evaluation involves self-assessment of outputs to ensure quality .
Pattern 5: Plan-and-Execute
Plan-and-execute architectures give you a checkpoint between planning and execution so you
can review the plan before running it .
Pattern 6: Reflection and Replanning
Reflection and replanning extend this further — when mid-execution findings change what's
needed, the system updates its plan rather than continuing down the wrong path .

lessons.title: Task Decomposition
lessons.content:
Task decomposition transforms static agent orchestration into adaptive workflows that respond to
actual request complexity .
Decomposition Granularity
Optimal granularity varies by task type :
Some tasks work better with a single agent
Others benefit from multi-agent decomposition
Over-decomposition adds overhead without adding quality
Task Boundaries
Task boundaries work best at natural capability interfaces where one agent's complete output is
what the next agent needs .

lessons.title: Multi-Agent Orchestration
lessons.content:
Orchestration Patterns
Pattern Description
Sequential Agents run one after another
Concurrent Agents run in parallel
Handoff Agents transfer tasks peer-to-peer
Magentic Designed for open-ended, complex problems without predetermined plans
Context Management in Multi-Agent Systems
AI agents often have limited context windows. This constraint can affect their ability to process
complex tasks, especially as context grows with each agent transition .
Mitigation strategies:
Use context compaction (summarization or selective pruning) between agents
Persist shared state externally for long-running tasks
Scope persisted state to the minimum necessary information

lessons.title: Reliability and Security
lessons.content:
Reliability Patterns
For multi-agent systems, implement :
Timeout and retry mechanisms
Graceful degradation
Error surfacing
Output validation before passing to next agent
Security Considerations
Implement :
Authentication between agents
Data privacy protections
Audit trails
Principle of least privilege
Content safety guardrails

Not To)

lessons.title: When to Use AI Agents
lessons.content:
AI agents are most effective in scenarios where tasks :
Criterion Description
Require integrating information From multiple sources or systems
Involve multiple steps Or decisions
Benefit from automation With minimal human oversight
Good Use Cases
Monitoring servers and fixing issues
Finding customers who overpaid and initiating refunds
Researching and synthesizing information
Coordinating complex workflows
When a Simple Query Suffices
If a task is straightforward and single-step (like "show latest sales figures"), a simple query or bot
might suffice .

lessons.title: The Risks of AI Agents
lessons.content:
The Verification Problem
One big risk area comes from the fact that it is often very easy to get agents to do certain types
of work for you. Because it is so easy, people may not put enough effort into verifying that it is
doing the right thing .
Bugs will be introduced, private data will get leaked — this is already happening .
The Human Error Problem
Agents aren't perfect. They might make mistakes because they are not well-trained. But even if
they are very competent, if a human doesn't use them appropriately or gives them an instruction
that is too vague, the AI agent could make a mistake because the human made a mistake .
The High-Stakes Problem
For cases that are high-stakes or safety-critical (like medicine, security, high-level business
policies), the technology might not be ready for AI to completely automate those processes .

lessons.title: Implementing Agents in Your Workplace
lessons.content:
Start Simple
Starting an agentic system should aim for simplicity. Begin with a basic implementation and add
complexity only with clear reasons. This keeps the system manageable and focused .
Human Oversight is Essential
While agents can help automate parts of workflows, the final outcome is still the responsibility of
humans. Before acting on information from an agent, you should :
Review the results
Verify important information
Review recommendations
Use business knowledge and judgment
The Framework for Assessment
A practical framework starts with the business need :
Question Consideration
Is it mainly helping a human, or acting toward an outcome? Assistant vs. Agent
Is the flow fixed, or does it need dynamic planning? Workflow vs. Agent
Question Consideration
Does it just generate/recommend, or also use tools and take actions? Passive vs. Active
How much human approval is needed? Autonomy level
What's the risk if it gets something wrong? Criticality

lessons.title: The Future of AI Agents
lessons.content:
The deployment of AI agents has recently exploded. A November 2025 report found that 35
percent of surveyed businesses had already deployed AI agents, while another 44 percent
planned to implement agentic AI soon .
What's Working
The area with the most success has been coding agents. This evolved from generative AI —
people trained language models on code, and then agents can learn by going through a feedback
loop where they try out different solutions and check to see if they got the answer right .
The Balance
There is always a balance between automating decision making versus simply assisting and
informing humans. Analytical AI methods that help predict possible outcomes are not agentic in
nature, but are very informative to human decision-makers .

lessons.title: What Are AI Agents?
lessons.content:
The Definition
AI agents are AI-powered assistants built into software applications that help users perform tasks
through natural language prompts. In the context of data visualization, these agents can:
Generate charts and graphs from natural language descriptions
Analyze data and provide insights
Suggest visualizations based on data patterns
Automate repetitive data analysis tasks

Microsoft Excel Copilot Data analysis, formula generation, chart suggestions
Microsoft Power BI Copilot Report creation, DAX generation, insights
Tableau Tableau Agent Visualization suggestions, calculations, insights
Why AI Agents Matter
AI agents are transforming how people interact with data by:
Lowering the barrier to complex analysis
Accelerating visualization creation
Enabling natural language interaction with data
Democratizing data insights for non-technical users

lessons.title: What is Generative AI?
lessons.content:
The Definition
Generative AI is a field of machine learning that develops and uses models for generating new
content . These models are often called large language models (LLMs) because of their large size
and ability to understand and generate natural language.
Traditional AI vs Generative AI
Aspect Traditional AI Generative AI
Primary Function Analyze, classify, predict Generate new content
Output Labels, numbers, predictions Text, images, audio, code
Training Custom models for specific tasks Pretrained on internet-scale data
Interaction Structured input Natural language prompts
Key Difference: Traditional AI builds custom models for specific predictions. Generative AI uses
pretrained models to generate content in response to user prompts .

lessons.title: The Main Types of Generative AI
lessons.content:
Text Generation
Some generative AI applications produce natural language outputs :
Professionally worded summaries
Rich descriptions of items
Ideas and brainstorming
Email drafts and reports
Example: Given the input "Give me three ideas for a healthy breakfast including peppers," a
generative AI application might produce detailed recipe suggestions .
Image Generation
Some generative AI applications produce image outputs from natural language inputs :
Virtual avatars for online accounts
Logos for businesses
Artistic inspiration for creators
Product designs
Example: "Create an image of an elephant eating a burger" produces a custom image .
Audio Generation
Some generative AI applications produce audio outputs :
Natural-sounding voices from text
Music in specific styles
Modified audio files
Code Generation
Some generative AI applications produce code from natural language inputs :
Quick implementations of common operations
Code translation between languages
Answers about technologies
Example: "Show me how to code a game of tic-tac-toe with C#" produces working code .

lessons.title: How We Got Here
lessons.content:
The Evolution of AI
Generative AI didn't appear overnight. It's the result of decades of research :
Era Development
Early AI Rules-based logic systems
Machine Learning Statistical learning from data
Deep Learning Neural networks with multiple layers
Transformers Architecture enabling today's LLMs
Generative AI Pretrained models generating content
The Transformer Breakthrough
A major innovation behind generative AI is the transformer architecture . Transformer-based
models offer:
Contextual understanding: Process entire documents, maintaining context
Scalability: Handle data in parallel, making them fast
Versatility: Work across text, images, and code

lessons.title: How Models Learn
lessons.content:
The Training Process
Generative AI models learn by analyzing huge volumes of data—a process called machine learning
:
1. Training: The model processes large datasets of content
2. Pattern Discovery: It identifies patterns and relationships
3. Generation: It uses learned patterns to produce new content
What Models Learn
At the core of generative AI, large language models (LLMs) encapsulate the linguistic and
semantic relationships between words and phrases . The model uses these relationships to:
Reason over natural language input
Generate meaningful and relevant responses

lessons.title: How Prompts Work
lessons.content:
The Prompt-Response Cycle
Generative AI applications rely on natural language inputs and produce variable outputs
depending on the prompt and context .
The process:
1. Prompt: You provide a natural language request
2. Parsing: The model parses the input into a form it can understand
3. Pattern Matching: It identifies matching patterns from training
4. Generation: It combines patterns to build the final output
Prompt Design
Creating a prompt to get the desired response is called prompt design . While it's a process of trial
and error, there are principles and strategies to guide the model.

lessons.title: What LLMs Can and Can't Do
lessons.content:
Capabilities
Capability Description
Writing Drafts, summaries, reports
Reading Comprehension, analysis
Chatting Conversational interaction
Coding Code generation and explanation
Reasoning Logical analysis of information
Limitations
Limitation Description
Hallucination May generate plausible but incorrect information
Context Window Limited amount of text it can process at once
Training Cutoff Doesn't know events after training date
Bias Reflects biases in training data
The Mental Model
Andrew Ng emphasizes understanding the limitations of LLMs as valuable for effective use . Think
of an LLM as a "thought partner"—helpful but requiring verification .

When using generative AI, consider:

Is it safe? Could this cause harm?
Who is accountable? Who takes responsibility?
Ethical Considerations
The course includes "Responsible AI" as a key topic . As generative AI becomes more powerful,
ethical use becomes more important.
